title: Strongyloidiasis in the immunocompetent: an overlooked infection
case_text:
A 58-year-old Hispanic female presented with complaints of generalized pruritus and abdominal discomfort for the past 4-5 months. She moved to the United States from Puerto Rico 32 years back, and her last visit to her country was 5 years before. She denied rashes, joint pains, fever, chills, weight loss, or change in bowel movements. There was no history of trauma, new medications, or recent travel. She was not immunocompromised, and there was no history of autoimmune diseases. Her generalized pruritus persisted despite avoiding any skin products and despite empiric treatment with antihistamines and antifungal shampoos.
She was afebrile and hemodynamically stable. No skin rash, dry skin, hair changes, or lymphadenopathy was noted. There was no excoriation or burrows suggestive of scabies. Physical examination was otherwise unremarkable.
Pertinent labs included white cell count of 8.8/microL (4,800-10,800/microL) with 18.6% eosinophils (0-6%). Hemoglobin was 13.2 g/dL (12-16 g/dL) with platelet count of 419,000/microL (130,000-400,000/microL). CRP was 1.05 mg/dL (0-0.7 mg/dL), but erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 10 mm/h (0-20 mm/h). Her renal function, liver function, and thyroid-stimulating hormone tests were within normal limits. Review of her previous records revealed that eosinophilia was present for the past 7 years suggesting a possibility of chronic parasitic infections, especially with her travel history. Strongyloides IgG antibody was high at 2.43 IV (<=1.49 IV) suggesting Strongyloides infection.
She was treated with ivermectin (200 microg/kg) for two consecutive days. On subsequent follow-up visit, her pruritus and abdominal discomfort had resolved along with the resolution of peripheral eosinophilia (eosinophil counts dropped from 18.7 to 1.7%). Follow-up serum IgG for Strongyloides was negative, as were stool tests for ova and parasites.

2. THE ADMISSION BREAKPOINT PRINCIPLE (CRITICAL):
   - The <case_prompt> represents what an emergency triage clinician knows on Day 1 BEFORE confirmatory tests return.
   - INCLUDE in <case_prompt>: Demographics, travel/occupational/vector exposures (freshwater contact, insect bites, animal exposure), symptom chronology, vital signs, physical exam findings, and initial triage laboratory/imaging results (CBC, platelets, basic metabolic panel, LFTs, urinalysis, plain chest radiograph, bedside ultrasound).
   - STRICTLY EXCLUDE from <case_prompt>:
     * Any mention of the disease name or pathogen genus/species (e.g., do not write "Leptospirosis", "Burkholderia", "Leishmania", "Paragonimus").
     * Confirmatory send-out PCR panels, serological titers, blood culture organism identifications, or biopsy histopathology.
     * The clinical outcome or treatment response (these belong in the diagnostic reasoning, not the presentation).

3. STRUCTURE OF <diagnostic_reasoning>:
   - Enumerate all alternative candidate diagnoses considered in the text.
   - For each candidate, provide a concise summary explaining why it was considered and why it was ruled out in this patient, followed by a direct verbatim quote from the article in quotation marks.
   - Conclude with the Diagnostic Pivot: the pivotal clinical and confirmatory turning point that established the confirmed diagnosis.

4. TARGET CANONICAL DISEASE:
   - The verified ground-truth disease for this patient is: Soil-Transmitted Helminths
   - Disease subtype / specific manifestation: strongyloidiasis in an immunocompetent patient
